title: LU Decomposition
description: Conceptual review of LU/PLU/LDU decomposition: triangular matrix properties, existence and uniqueness, permutation matrices, and why the decomposition is worth computing (Anton 9.1).

questions.prompt: The product of two lower triangular matrices (of the same size) is lower triangular.
explanations: Triangular matrices are closed under multiplication: multiplying out $L_1 L_2$, every entry above the diagonal is a sum of products where at least one factor is 0, so it stays lower triangular.

questions.prompt: The product of two upper triangular matrices (of the same size) is upper triangular.
explanations: Same closure property as the lower triangular case, just reflected: the zero pattern above/below the diagonal is preserved under multiplication.

questions.prompt: The sum of two lower triangular matrices is lower triangular.
explanations: Addition is entrywise, so if both matrices have 0's above the diagonal, their sum does too.

questions.prompt: The inverse of an invertible lower triangular matrix is lower triangular.
explanations: This is exactly why solving $Ly=b$ by forward substitution works, and it's part of why $L^{-1}$ shows up as lower triangular when you compute $A^{-1}=U^{-1}L^{-1}$.

questions.prompt: The inverse of an invertible upper triangular matrix is upper triangular.
explanations: Mirror image of the lower triangular case — back substitution on $Ux=y$ only works because $U^{-1}$ is upper triangular too.

questions.prompt: A matrix that is both lower triangular and upper triangular at the same time must be a diagonal matrix.
explanations: Lower triangular forces all entries above the diagonal to be 0; upper triangular forces all entries below the diagonal to be 0. The only entries left are on the diagonal.

questions.prompt: If an invertible matrix $A$ has an LU decomposition, then $A$ has a unique LDU decomposition $A=LDU$, where $L$ and $U$ are required to have 1's on their diagonals and $D$ is a diagonal matrix of the pivots.
explanations: This is exactly the fix for LU's non-uniqueness: once you force $L$ and $U$ to have unit diagonals and pull every pivot out into $D$, there's only one way to split $A$ up this way.

questions.prompt: Every square matrix has a PLU decomposition $PA=LU$ for some permutation matrix $P$, even if $A$ is singular.
explanations: Partial pivoting can always be carried out on a square matrix — you just swap in a nonzero entry when you can, and skip a column entirely (leaving a 0 pivot in $U$) when an entire column below is already 0. $L$ still comes out unit lower triangular either way.

questions.prompt: Every invertible matrix has a standard LU decomposition $A=LU$ (no row swaps needed).
explanations: Not true — $A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$ is invertible, but its very first pivot spot is 0, so elimination breaks immediately and a row swap is required. Invertibility guarantees a PLU decomposition, not a swap-free LU one.

questions.prompt: The determinant of a triangular matrix equals the sum of its diagonal entries.
explanations: That's the trace, not the determinant. The determinant of a triangular matrix is the *product* of its diagonal entries.

questions.prompt: If $PA=LU$ (with $L$ the unit lower triangular matrix from the elimination method used in class), then $\det(A)=\pm\det(U)$, with the sign coming from the number of row swaps in $P$.
explanations: Since $\det(L)=1$ (unit diagonal) and $\det(P)=\pm1$, taking determinants of $PA=LU$ gives $\pm\det(A)=\det(U)$, i.e. $\det(A)=\pm\det(U)$.

questions.prompt: A permutation matrix is always invertible, and its inverse equals its transpose.
explanations: Permutation matrices just reorder rows of the identity, so they're always invertible, and undoing a permutation is the same as transposing it: $P^{-1}=P^{T}$.

questions.prompt: In the elimination step $R_{\text{row}}\to R_{\text{row}}-m\cdot R_{\text{col}}$, the entry recorded in $L$ at that position is $-m$, the negative of the multiplier.
explanations: It's the other way around — the entry recorded in $L$ is $+m$, the multiplier itself. (The elementary matrix that performs the elimination step has $-m$ in it; $L$ is built from the *inverses* of those elementary matrices, which flips the sign back to $+m$.)

questions.prompt: Once a matrix's LU decomposition is known, solving $Ax=b$ for a new $b$ only requires two triangular solves (forward then back substitution), not a fresh elimination from scratch.
explanations: That's the entire point of computing $L$ and $U$ in the first place — the expensive elimination work happens once, and every new $b$ after that is cheap.

questions.prompt: If a row swap is required partway through elimination, only the rows of $U$ need to be swapped — any multipliers already recorded in $L$ are unaffected.
explanations: The already-recorded multiplier entries in $L$'s earlier columns have to swap right along with the rows, or the final $L$ and $U$ won't actually satisfy $PA=LU$. This is the easiest step to forget.

questions.prompt: Two different pairs $(L,U)$ — each satisfying only “$L$ lower triangular, $U$ upper triangular, $LU=A$” — can have different diagonal entries in $L$.
explanations: Since the definition doesn't pin the diagonal down, you can rescale a row of $L$ by any nonzero $c$ and the matching row of $U$ by $1/c$ and still get a valid decomposition of the same $A$. That's exactly why LU decompositions aren't unique in general.

questions.prompt: If $A$ is invertible and $A=LU$, then $A^{-1}=U^{-1}L^{-1}$.
explanations: This follows from the general rule $(XY)^{-1}=Y^{-1}X^{-1}$ applied to $X=L$, $Y=U$ — and it's useful in its own right, since $U^{-1}$ and $L^{-1}$ are each cheap triangular inverses.

questions.explanation: Solving for $A$ gives $A=(E_k\cdots E_1)^{-1}U = E_1^{-1}\cdots E_k^{-1}U$, so $L=E_1^{-1}\cdots E_k^{-1}$ — the product of the inverse elementary matrices, in reverse order.

questions.prompt: In the decomposition $A=LDU$ (with $L$ and $U$ unit triangular), $D$ is a _____ matrix containing the pivots.
questions.explanation: $D$ collects all the pivot values on its diagonal, with 0's everywhere else — that's what lets $L$ and $U$ both be normalized to unit diagonals without losing any information.

questions.prompt: When a row swap is required during elimination, we track it with a _____ matrix, giving $PA=LU$ instead of $A=LU$.
questions.explanation: $P$ is built from the identity matrix by making the same row swaps you performed during elimination.

questions.prompt: If the elimination step $R_{\text{row}}\to R_{\text{row}}-m\cdot R_{\text{col}}$ is used to zero out a below-pivot entry, the corresponding entry recorded in $L$ is _____.
questions.explanation: $L$ stores the multiplier itself (not its negative) in the position it came from — that's what makes $L$ fall out for free as you eliminate.

questions.prompt: The determinant of a triangular matrix equals the product of its _____ entries.
questions.explanation: Expanding the determinant of a triangular matrix along the first column (or by cofactor expansion in general) collapses to just the product down the diagonal.

questions.prompt: The inverse of a permutation matrix $P$ is always equal to its _____.
questions.explanation: Permutation matrices are orthogonal: $P^{-1}=P^{T}$, so undoing a permutation is as easy as flipping rows and columns.

questions.prompt: Every square matrix — invertible or not — has a valid _____ decomposition, using a permutation matrix if row swaps are needed along the way.
questions.explanation: Partial pivoting always succeeds on a square matrix, even a singular one, so $PA=LU$ always exists — that's a stronger guarantee than plain $A=LU$.

questions.prompt: The product of two upper triangular matrices is always _____ triangular.
questions.explanation: Triangular matrices are closed under multiplication, and upper stays upper.

questions.prompt: If $L_1$ and $L_2$ are invertible lower triangular matrices, then $L_1^{-1}$ and $L_1 L_2$ are both _____ triangular.
questions.explanation: Lower triangular matrices are closed under both inversion and multiplication.

questions.prompt: Taking determinants in $PA=LU$ gives $\det(P)\det(A)=\det(L)\det(U)$. Since $\det(L)=1$ for the unit lower triangular $L$ from class's elimination method, this simplifies to $\det(A)=\pm\det(X)$, where $X=$ _____.
The main computational payoff of an LU decomposition is that solving $Ax=b$ for many different $b$'s only needs two cheap _____ solves each time, instead of a full elimination from scratch.
questions.explanation: Forward substitution on $Ly=b$ (or $Ly=Pb$) and back substitution on $Ux=y$ are both fast — that's the entire reason LU decomposition is worth computing once and reusing.

questions.prompt: A matrix that is simultaneously lower triangular and upper triangular must be a _____ matrix.
questions.explanation: Being lower triangular kills everything above the diagonal; being upper triangular kills everything below it. Only the diagonal survives.

questions.prompt: In building $L$ from elimination, each below-diagonal entry of $L$ records a _____ used to eliminate that position.
questions.explanation: Instead of throwing the multiplier away after using it to eliminate an entry, you record it directly into $L$ in that same spot.
